solution: The question says only that the circles "touch each other", so both cases are possible. Touching externally, the distance between the centres is the sum of the radii, \(5.5 + 3.3 = 8.8\) cm; touching internally, it is the difference of the radii, \(5.5 - 3.3 = 2.2\) cm. \(\therefore\) the answer is 8.8 or 2.2 cm.

solution: If a circle touches all four sides of \(\square\)ABCD, then by the tangent segment theorem \(AB + CD = AD + BC\). For a parallelogram \(AB = CD\) and \(AD = BC\), so \(2AB = 2AD\), that is all four sides are equal. \(\therefore\) the parallelogram must be a rhombus. (A square is a special rhombus, but the parallelogram need not be a square, so 'rhombus' is the answer that must hold.)

solution: The radius drawn to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent, so \(r^2 = (12.5)^2 - 12^2 = 156.25 - 144 = 12.25\), giving \(r = 3.5\) cm. \(\therefore\) the diameter is \(2 \times 3.5 = 7\) cm.

solution: [Textbook note: the printed answer key on p.165 gives (B) Two; the correct answer is (C) Three.] For two circles touching externally the distance between the centres equals the sum of the radii. In that position there are two direct common tangents (one on each side of the line of centres) and exactly one more common tangent, the one drawn at the point of contact itself, giving three in all. The chapter shows two of these three for this very configuration: fig 3.24 draws the common tangent at the point of contact of two externally touching circles, and Practice set 3.2 Q.5 (fig 3.28) draws a direct common tangent to two externally touching circles.

solution: \(\angle ACB\) is inscribed in arc ACB, so it intercepts the other arc AB. By the inscribed angle theorem \(m(\text{arc AB}) = 2 \times 65^\circ = 130^\circ\). \(\therefore m(\text{arc ACB}) = 360^\circ - 130^\circ = 230^\circ\).

solution: \(\angle A\) and \(\angle C\) are opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, so \(\angle A + \angle C = 180^\circ\). Given \(2\angle A = 3\angle C\), so \(\angle A = \dfrac{3}{2}\angle C\). Then \(\dfrac{3}{2}\angle C + \angle C = 180^\circ\), that is \(\dfrac{5}{2}\angle C = 180^\circ\) and \(\angle C = 72\).

solution: Arc AB and arc BC have only point B in common, so \(m(\text{arc ABC}) = 120^\circ + 120^\circ = 240^\circ\) and therefore \(m(\text{arc AC}) = 360^\circ - 240^\circ = 120^\circ\). All three arcs have measure \(120^\circ\), so the three chords AB, BC and CA are congruent. \(\therefore \triangle ABC\) is an equilateral triangle.

solution: Seg XZ is a diameter and Y is an interior point of the circle. Let ray XY meet the circle at M, so X-Y-M and \(\angle XMZ = 90^\circ\) (angle inscribed in a semicircle). \(\angle XYZ\) is an exterior angle of \(\triangle YMZ\) at Y, so \(\angle XYZ = \angle YMZ + \angle YZM > 90^\circ\). Hence \(\angle XYZ\) is always obtuse: statement (i) is true, (ii) is true, (iii) is true and (iv) is false. \(\therefore\) only three of the statements are true.
